South Vietnam: 23,346 killed {{cite book|last=Clarke|first=Jeffrey|title=United States Army in Vietnam: Advice and Support: The Final Years, 1965-1973|publisher= Center of Military History, United States Army|year=1988|url=https://history.army.mil/html/books/091/91-3/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120913060006/http://www.history.army.mil/html/books/091/91-3/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 13, 2012|isbn=978-1518612619}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|275}} | casualties2 = Unknown | yearcost1 = }} {{Campaignbox Vietnam War}} The [[United States]] continued its unilateral withdrawal of forces from [[South Vietnam]] notwithstanding the lack of progress at the [[Paris Peace Talks]]. The removal of Prince [[Norodom Sihanouk]] from power in [[Cambodia]] in March and his replacement by General [[Lon Nol]], began the [[Cambodian Civil War]]. South Vietnamese and U.S. forces [[Cambodian campaign|entered Cambodia]] in late April to attack [[People's Army of Vietnam]] (PAVN) and [[Vietcong]] (VC) bases and supply lines there which had long been used to support the insurgency in South Vietnam. The expansion of the war revitalized the antiwar movement in the U.S. and led to the [[Kent State shootings]] and [[Jackson State killings]] in May. While U.S. ground forces withdrew from Cambodia at the end of June and legislation was passed to prevent their reintroduction, the South Vietnamese conducted operations in Cambodia for the rest of the year and the U.S. provided air support and military aid to the Cambodian government. Despite this support the Cambodians lost control of vast areas of the country to the PAVN. Within South Vietnam the second half of the year saw a reduction in large U.S. operations with the focus shifting to pacification and population security and supporting [[Vietnamization]]. The PAVN/VC generally reverted to sapper attacks and attacks by fire but they fought hard to defend their base areas and infiltration routes. ==January== ;2-3 January [[People's Army of Vietnam]] (PAVN) forces attacked a U.S. [[23rd Infantry Division (United States)|23rd Infantry Division]] night defensive position near [[Đức Phổ Base Camp]]. In the four hour battle 29 PAVN and seven U.S. soldiers were killed.{{cite book|last=Willbanks|first=James|title=Vietnam War Almanac: An In-Depth Guide to the Most Controversial Conflict in American History|publisher=Simon and Schuster|year=2013|isbn=9781626365285}}{{rp|325}} ;6 January Under the cover of monsoon rains the [[Vietcong]] (VC) 409th Battalion attacked the [[1st Battalion, 7th Marines]] at [[Firebase Ross]] with mortars and sappers penetrating the wire. The attack was repulsed by 04:00 with 13 Marines and 38 VC killed.{{cite book|last=Cosmas|first=Graham|title=US Marines in Vietnam Vietnamization and Redeployment 1970-1971|publisher=History and Museums Division Headquarters United States Marine Corps|year=1986|isbn=9781494287498|url=https://www.usmcu.edu/Portals/218/US%20Marines%20In%20Vietnam%20Vietmanization%20and%20Redeployment%201970-1971%20PCN%2019000309600.pdf}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|48–50}} ;8 January [[Leaders of South Vietnam|President of South Vietnam]] [[Nguyễn Văn Thiệu]] announced that it would be impossible for U.S. forces to fully withdraw from South Vietnam by the end of 1970 and called for increased aid and training and phased U.S. withdrawal over several years.{{rp|325}} ;16 January The VC attacked a refugee camp on the [[Batangan Peninsula]] killing 16 civilians and wounding 21.{{rp|325}} ;18 January VC bombs exploded at the [[Thủ Đức Military Academy]] killing 18 people and wounding 33.{{rp|325}} ;18-24 January The first Tour de Vietnam cycle race in 14 years began, following a {{convert|500|mi}} course from [[Nha Trang]] to [[Long Xuyên (city)|Long Xuyên]]. The race was to demonstrate the extent of government control over the countryside, however the competitors were escorted by armored vehicles and helicopter gunships.{{cite news|newspaper=the New York Times|title=Cyclists race in Vietnam with politics in tandem|date=19 January 1970|page=3}} ;19 January to 22 July The 1st Brigade, [[5th Infantry Division (United States)|5th Infantry Division]] launched [[Operation Green River]] in [[Quảng Trị Province]]. The operation results in 106 PAVN soldiers killed and 37 U.S. killed.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/2624/26240106001.pdf|title= Operational Report - Lessons Learned Headquarters, 1st Infantry Brigade, 5th Infantry Division, Period Ending 31 July 1970 |publisher=Department of the Army Headquarters, 1st Infantry Brigade, 5th Infantry Division|date=25 January 1971|access-date=25 June 2020|page=3}}{{PD-notice}} ;21 January A PAVN/VC artillery attack on [[Bien Hoa Air Base]] damaged a [[Fairchild C-123 Provider|C–123]], a [[de Havilland Canada DHC-4 Caribou|C–7]] and a [[Bell UH-1 Iroquois|UH–1]].{{cite book|last=Nalty|first=Bernard|title=The United States Air Force in Southeast Asia: The War in South Vietnam Air War over South Vietnam 1968–1975|publisher=Air Force History and Museums Program|year=2000|url=http://www.afhso.af.mil/shared/media/document/AFD-100924-004.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130216072651/http://www.afhso.af.mil/shared/media/document/AFD-100924-004.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 16, 2013|isbn=9781478118640}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|246}} A box of [[M29 mortar|81 mm mortar]] ammunition exploded at Firebase Nancy, {{convert|20|mi}} north-northeast of [[Xuân Lộc District|Xuân Lộc]], killed 13 soldiers of the U.S. 4th Battalion, [[12th Infantry Regiment (United States)|12th Infantry Regiment]].{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=72 of enemy reported killed in Delta|date=23 January 1970|page=14}} ;22 January A PAVN/VC attack on a [[Republic of Vietnam Marine Division]] (VNMC) base in the [[Mekong Delta]] results in 72 PAVN/VC and 15 VNMC killed. ;28 January [[United States Air Force]] (USAF) jets attacked an [[S-75 Dvina|SA-2]] missile site near the [[Mụ Giạ Pass]] after it fired on a U.S. reconnaissance jet. One USAF [[Republic F-105 Thunderchief|F-105G]] [[Wild Weasel]] was shot down during the raid. ''Jolly Green 71'' an [[Sikorsky MH-53|HH-53B]] combat search and rescue helicopter was shot down by a missile fired from a [[Mig-21]] piloted by [[Vu Ngoc Dinh]] of the [[Vietnam People's Air Force]] [[921st Fighter Regiment]] as it attempted to rescue the aircrew. The 6-man crew were all killed.{{Cite web |url=http://www.acig.org/artman/publish/article_246.shtml |title=Vietnamese Air-to-Air Victories, Part 2 |access-date=10 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130304225827/http://www.acig.org/artman/publish/article_246.shtml |archive-date=4 March 2013 |url-status=usurped}}{{rp|326}} A [[Gallup (company)|Gallup]] poll showed that 65% of Americans approved of [[President of the United States|President]] [[Richard Nixon]]'s handling of the war.{{rp|326}} ;30 January Nixon stated that [[Vietnamization]] was "irreversible" but that he would respond forcefully to any increase in North Vietnamese military activity.{{rp|326}} ==February== ;3 February The [[United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations]] led by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[United States Senate|Senator]] [[J. William Fulbright]] reopened hearings on the war. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Senator [[Charles Goodell]] described Vietnamization as "a great public relations success" but "not a true policy of disengagement."{{rp|327}} ;5 February Starting at 18:00, Allied forces began a 24-hour [[Tết]] ceasefire. U.S. jets attacked North Vietnamese antiaircraft positions in the [[Ban Karai Pass]] after they had fired on U.S. reconnaissance jets.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|date=6 February 1970|title=U.S. again bombs North as reconnaissance planes are fired on|page=3}} U.S. helicopter gunships accidentally attacked [[South Vietnamese Regional Forces]] test-firing a machine-gun killing eight and wounding 31. ;10 February [[United States Secretary of Defense]] [[Melvin Laird]] in [[Saigon]] for a fact-finding mission said that he was satisfied with the current pace of Vietnamization.{{rp|327}} ;12 February The PAVN 31st Regiment ambushed a 1st Battalion, 7th Marines patrol near Firebase Ross in the [[Quế Sơn District|Quế Sơn valley]]. The U.S. 3rd Battalion, [[21st Infantry Regiment (United States)|21st Infantry Regiment]] was sent to support the Marines. U.S. losses were 13 killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Foe kills 14 G.I.s in Danang ambush|date=22 February 1970|page=1}}{{rp|50–1}} ;14 February A Gallup poll showed that 55% of Americans opposed an immediate withdrawal from South Vietnam compared to 35% in favor.{{rp|327}} ;16 February Two ARVN [[Vietnamese Rangers|Ranger]] battalions and the 1st Armored Brigade reported killing 280 PAVN and capturing 36 after a series of encounters over five days {{convert|18|mi}} south of [[Da Nang]]. ARVN losses were 23 killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Allied say units kill 145 of foe|date=16 February 1970|page=8}} ;17 February [[Military Police Corps (United States)|Military Policemen]] were called to a murder scene in an apartment at [[Fort Bragg]]. [[United States Army Special Forces|Special Forces]] [[Captain (United States O-3)|Captain]] [[Jeffrey R. MacDonald]] claimed that four intruders attacked his family killing his pregnant wife and two young daughters. The case remains one of the most litigated murder cases in American criminal history.{{cite book|first1=Joe|last1=Nickell|first2=John F.|last2=Fischer|title=Crime Science: Methods of Forensic Detection|publisher=[[University Press of Kentucky]]|location=Lexington, Kentucky|date=1998|isbn=978-0-813-12091-1|pages=43–9}} Testifying before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, [[William Colby]], head of [[Civil Operations and Revolutionary Development Support]] (CORDS) denied that the [[Phoenix Program]] was an assassination program, while acknowledging that "some illegal killings" had taken place. Colby stated that in 1969 19,534 suspected VC cadres had been "neutralized" of which 6,187 had been killed, 8,515 captured and 4,832 [[Chieu Hoi|defected]]. Colby said "I am neither optimistic nor pessimistic about the future of this program or Vietnam."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. aide in Saigon denies "counter-terror" charge|author=Tad Szulc|date=17 February 1970|page=1}} ;18 February Sergeant Michael Mullen was killed by shrapnel from friendly artillery fire while serving with the [[6th Infantry Regiment (United States)|6th Infantry Regiment]] in [[Quảng Tín Province]]. His death prompted his mother [[Peg Mullen]] to become an antiwar activist who was profiled by journalist [[C.D.B. Bryan]] in [[The New Yorker]] in 1976 and the story was subsequently made into the 1979 telemovie [[Friendly Fire (1979 film)|''Friendly Fire'']].{{cite news|title=Peg Mullen, 92, Who Fanned Her Anger Over Son's Death Into Antiwar Drive, Dies|newspaper=The New York Times|author=Douglas Martin|date=5 October 2009|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/06/us/06mullen.html}} USAF [[Boeing B-52 Stratofortress|B-52]] bombers were reported to be bombing PAVN and [[Pathet Lao]] forces on the [[Plain of Jars]], the first time the heavy bombers had been used in northern [[Laos]].{{rp|328}} ;19 February In the [[Son Thang massacre]] five U.S. Marines killed five Vietnamese women and 11 children in Sơn Thắng, Quế Sơn Valley. Four of the Marines were charged with murder, two were acquitted and two convicted but only served sentences of one year.{{rp|345–7}} ;21 February Despite the U.S. bombing, PAVN and Pathet Lao forces captured [[Xiangkhouang]] airfield and most of the Plain of Jars while the [[Royal Lao Army]] forces retreated west.{{rp|329}} PAVN forces ambushed a mechanized infantry unit from the [[196th Infantry Brigade (United States)|196th Light Infantry Brigade]] in the Quế Sơn valley, killing 14 and wounding 29 in a five hour battle. PAVN losses were four killed. ;27 February A PAVN/VC rocket attack on Bien Hoa Air Base damaged three [[Cessna A-37 Dragonfly|A-37s]], two [[North American F-100 Super Sabre|F-100s]] and a C-7. Two USAF personnel were killed in these attacks and 74 wounded.{{rp|246}} ==March== ;9 March Operational control of U.S. forces in [[I Corps (South Vietnam)|I Corps]] passed from [[III Marine Amphibious Corps]] to [[XXIV Corps (United States)|XXIV Corps]].{{rp|443}} ;11 March Anti-Vietnamese demonstrations erupted in [[Phnom Penh]], [[Cambodia]] while head of state Prince [[Norodom Sihanouk]] was touring Europe, the Soviet Union and China. Crowds attacked the North Vietnamese and VC embassies.{{rp|330}} ; 12 March Cambodian prime minister [[Lon Nol]] closed the port of [[Sihanoukville Autonomous Port|Sihanoukville]] to the North Vietnamese and demanded that all PAVN and VC forces withdraw from Cambodian soil within 72 hours (on 15 March) or face military action.{{rp|330}} ;14 March The first [[FTA Show]] is performed in [[Fayetteville, North Carolina]], near Fort Bragg.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=500 G.I.'s at Debut of Antiwar Show|last=Wooten|first=James T.|date=15 March 1971}} ;14 March – 12 April In the [[SS Columbia Eagle incident|SS ''Columbia Eagle'' incident]], two crewmembers seized the {{SS|Columbia Eagle||2}} with the threat of a bomb and handgun and forced the captain to sail towards Cambodia. Twenty-four of the crew were forced to abandon the ship in lifeboats, while the remaining 13 sailed the ship into Cambodian waters and the two mutineers Clyde McKay Jr. and Alvin Glatkowski surrendered to the Cambodia government which gave them asylum. The mutineers were later arrested and imprisoned in Cambodia, but released later in the year. Glatowski eventually turned himself in to the U.S. Embassy, was extradited to the U.S. and served seven years in prison, while McKay sought refuge with the [[Khmer Rouge]] who apparently killed him.{{cite book|last1=Lipsman|first1=Samuel|last2=Doyle|first2=Edward|title=Fighting for Time (The Vietnam Experience)|publisher=Boston Publishing Company|year=1984|isbn=9780939526079}}{{rp|141}} ;16 March A U.S. Navy [[Lockheed EC-121 Warning Star|EC-121 Warning Star]] crashed on landing at [[Da Nang Air Base]]. The aircraft struck a hangar and caught fire killing 22 of the 31-man crew.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010812.pdf|title=Headquarters MACV Monthly Summary March 1970|publisher=Headquarters United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam|date=11 July 1970|access-date=14 July 2020|pages=34–5}}{{PD-notice}} ;17 March The [[William R. Peers|Peers Commission]] presented their report on the [[Mỹ Lai massacre]]. The report found that members of the 23rd Infantry Division had killed at least 175–200 Vietnamese men, women and children and that senior officers at brigade and divisional levels had participated in covering-up the incident.{{rp|330}} ;18 March The Cambodian National Assembly [[1970 Cambodian coup d'état|voted to remove]] Sihanouk from power with Lon Nol taking the powers of the Head of State on an emergency basis.{{rp|330–1}} ;19-30 March Fearing a joint ARVN–Cambodian attack [[Central Office for South Vietnam]] began moving from the Cambodia-South Vietnam border area into [[Kratié Province]], Cambodia.{{cite book|last1=Tảng|first1=Truong Như|last2=Chanoff|first2=David|title=A Vietcong memoir|publisher=Harcourt Brace Jovanovich|year=1985|isbn=978015193636-6|page=177}} ;20 March The PAVN attacked [[Firebase Granite]], the attack was repulsed with 10 U.S. and 10 PAVN killed.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2519&dat=19700320&id=y3FeAAAAIBAJ&pg=3133,2658705&hl=en|title=North Vietnamese sappers attack jungle firebase|publisher=Observer-Reporter|date=20 March 1970|access-date=14 July 2020}} ;21 March North Vietnamese [[Prime Minister of Vietnam|Prime Minister]] [[Phạm Văn Đồng]] flew to [[Beijing]] to meet with [[Zhou Enlai]] and Sihanouk. Sihanouk agreed to accept the leadership of anti-Lon Nol forces under the umbrella of the [[National United Front of Kampuchea]] (FUNK).{{rp|331}} ;22 March The VC bombed a [[Buddhist]] meeting in [[Hóc Môn District]] killing 14 civilians and wounding 20.{{rp|331}} ;23 March [[File:Mao Sihanouk.jpg|thumb|right|Norodom Sihanouk in Beijing in 1965]] Sihanouk on Beijing radio called for a general uprising against Lon Nol and the formation of FUNK.{{rp|331}} ;25 March North Vietnam withdrew its diplomats from Cambodia.{{rp|331}} ;26 March North Vietnam refused an offer by South Vietnam for the release and repatriation of 343 wounded or ill [[prisoners of war]], declaring that there were no members of the PAVN in the south. The North Vietnamese representatives at the Paris Peace Talks asserted that the captives were, instead, "illegally arrested patriots" from among South Vietnamese citizens rebelling against the Saigon government.{{cite news|title=Reds Won't Take Own Sick POWs|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|date=27 March 1970|page=6}} The South Vietnamese Government began the [[Land reform in South Vietnam|''Land to the Tiller'' program]] of land reform designed to redistribute land to tenant farmers and undermine support for the VC.{{cite journal|last=Prosterman|first=Roy|title=Land-to-the-Tiller in South Vietnam : The Tables Turn|journal=Asian Survey |volume=10 |issue=8|pages=751–764|date=August 1970|doi=10.2307/2642811 |jstor=2642811 }} ;27-8 March ARVN Rangers with armored cavalry support and support from U.S. helicopter gunships made the first large-scale South Vietnamese attack into Cambodia attacking a PAVN base in [[Kandal Province]], killing 53 PAVN and capturing one for the loss of three ARVN killed.{{rp|331}} ;28 March The White House announced that based on the judgment of commanders in the field, U.S. forces could cross into Cambodia in response to PAVN/VC threats. The White House denied that this represented any change in policy or widening of the war.{{rp|331}} A U.S. Navy [[McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II|F-4 Phantom II]] shot down a VPAF [[Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21|MiG-21]] while escorting a reconnaissance jet near [[Thanh Hóa province|Thanh Hóa]] in the first aerial engagement since the November 1968 bombing halt.{{rp|332}} ;29 March The PAVN 272nd Regiment hit [[Firebase Jay]] with mortar, rocket and recoilless rifle fire hitting the command post and knocking out communications. The base was occupied by Companies A and E, 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry, [[12th Field Artillery Regiment (United States)#2d Battalion|B Battery, 2nd Battalion, 12th Artillery]] and [[19th Field Artillery Regiment (United States)|B Battery, 2nd Battalion, 19th Artillery]]. The PAVN then launched infantry attacks on the base perimeter but were beaten back by dawn. U.S. losses were 13 killed, while 74 PAVN dead were found in and around the base.{{cite book|last=Laurence|first=John|title=The Cat from Hue|url=https://archive.org/details/catfromhuvietn00laur|url-access=registration|publisher=Public Affairs|year=2001|isbn=1586481606}}{{rp|617–8}} The PAVN launched Campaign ''X'' against the Cambodian [[Khmer National Armed Forces]] (FANK), quickly seizing large portions of the eastern and northeastern parts of the country, isolating and besieging or overrunning a number of Cambodian cities including [[Kampong Cham (city)|Kampong Cham]].{{cite book|last=Sak|first=Sutsakhan|title=The Khmer Republic at war and the final collapse|publisher=United States Army Center of Military History|year=1984|isbn=9781780392585}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|61}} ==April == ;1 April [[199th Infantry Brigade (United States)|199th Infantry Brigade]] commander Brigadier General [[William R. Bond]] was killed by sniper fire in [[Bình Thủy District]].{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010803.pdf|title=Headquarters MACV Monthly Summary April 1970|publisher=Headquarters United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam|date=17 August 1970|access-date=4 July 2020}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|12}} The PAVN hit [[Firebase Illingworth]] with over 300 rounds of mortar and recoilless rifle fire and then assaulted the base with a force of over 400 troops. The base was defended by Companies C and E, 2nd Battalion, 8th Cavalry, [[2nd Field Artillery Regiment (United States)|B Battery, 5th Battalion, 2nd Artillery]], [[30th Field Artillery Regiment (United States)|A Battery, 1st Battalion, 30th Artillery]], [[32nd Field Artillery Regiment|A Battery, 2nd Battalion, 32nd Artillery]] and [[77th Field Artillery Regiment|B Battery, 1st Battalion, 77th Artillery]]. During the attack an ammunition dump containing over 190 rounds exploded. By 05:00 the attack had been repulsed at a cost of 24 U.S. killed and 54 wounded and 88 PAVN killed.{{cite web |url=https://www.army.mil/article/36723/Battle_survivors_reunite_40_years_later_at_Fort_Sill_monument/|title=Battle survivors reunite 40 years later at Fort Sill monument|publisher=US Army |date=1 April 2010 |access-date=14 July 2020}} [[File:Song Mao, January 1967.png|thumb|right|Song Mao Base Camp]] Three PAVN battalions attacked [[Song Mao Base Camp]] which was defended by the U.S. [[1st Cavalry Regiment (United States)|2nd Squadron, 1st Cavalry]] and the ARVN 44th Regiment, [[23rd Division (South Vietnam)|23rd Division]]. The attack was repulsed resulting in two U.S., two ARVN and 151 PAVN killed. ;1 April to 8 May The PAVN besiege [[Dak Seang Camp]]. On 15 April 1970 the [[170th Assault Helicopter Company]] dropped the 3rd Battalion, 42nd ARVN Regiment into a landing zone near Dak Seang, resulting in the loss of two helicopters. ;1 April to 5 September [[Operation Texas Star]] was a military operation of the U.S. [[101st Airborne Division]] and the [[Army of the Republic of Vietnam]] (ARVN) [[1st Division (South Vietnam)|1st Division]] against PAVN logistics routes and bases in the [[A Shau Valley]] and the mountains east of the valley. The operation culminated in the [[Battle of Fire Support Base Ripcord]].{{cite book|last=Stanton|first=Shelby L.|title=Vietnam order of battle|edition=2003|year=2003|publisher=Stackpole Books|isbn=0-811700712|page=13}} The operation resulted in 1,782 PAVN killed and five captured, U.S. losses were 386 killed and ARVN losses were 370 killed.{{cite book|last=Olson|first=James S.|title=In Country: The Illustrated Encyclopedia of the Vietnam War|date=2008|publisher=Metro Books|isbn=9781435111844}} ;4 April A group of 50,000 demonstrators picketed in Washington D.C. in the "March for Victory", organized by fundamentalist radio evangelist [[Carl McIntire]]. The marchers, mostly middle-aged white Americans, protested Nixon's decision to reduce the American commitment rather than to take the war into North Vietnam.{{cite news|title='Win In Viet' March Attracts 50,000|newspaper=Pittsburgh Press|date=5 April 1970|page=2}} ;5 April Photojournalist [[Gilles Caron]] disappeared on [[National Highway 1 (Cambodia)|Highway 1]] in Cambodia. He was the first of 25 journalists to disappear or be killed by the Khmer Rouge/PAVN between 5 April and 28 October 1970.{{cite book|last=Volkert|first=Kurt|title=A Cambodian Odyssey: and The Deaths of 25 Journalists |publisher=iUniverse|year=2001|isbn=9780595166060|page=187}} ;6 April Photojournalists [[Sean Flynn (photojournalist)|Sean Flynn]] and [[Dana Stone]] disappeared on Highway 1 in Cambodia. Later investigations revealed that they were captured by the PAVN and then handed over to the Khmer Rouge who executed them.{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/asia/how-errol-flynns-son-was-lost-in-cambodia-ndash-all-but-a-pile-of-bones-1931662.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220501/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/asia/how-errol-flynns-son-was-lost-in-cambodia-ndash-all-but-a-pile-of-bones-1931662.html |archive-date=2022-05-01 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=How Errol Flynn's son was lost in Cambodia – all but a pile of bones|date=31 March 2010|publisher=independent.co.uk|access-date=9 July 2020}}{{cbignore}} ;6-10 April The PAVN/VC attacked [[Khmer National Army]] (ANK) forces near Chiphou in [[Svay Rieng Province]] killing 20 with 30 more missing. The ANK claimed to have killed 300 PAVN/VC on 9 April, but the ANK then withdrew all its forces from the [[Parrot's Beak, Cambodia|Parrot's Beak]] region of Svay Rieng Province abandoning it to the PAVN/VC and forming a new defensive line at Prasot village, where the ANK killed numerous ethnic Vietnamese.{{rp|333}} ;7 April Nixon awarded 21 posthumous [[Medal of Honor|Medals of Honor]] to U.S. servicemen killed in the war.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=21 G.I.s awarded Medals of Honor posthumously by President|date=7 April 1970|page=3}} ;10 April [[File:NARA photo 111-CCV-627-CC64462.jpg|thumb|right|U.S. artillery at Mai Loc Camp]] Following a mortar and [[rocket-propelled grenade]] barrage, PAVN sappers attacked [[Mai Loc Camp]] which was defended by CIDG forces and a U.S. artillery unit. The PAVN withdrew with 19 dead, while U.S. losses were six and 14 CIDG were killed.{{cite news|title=Viet Reds overrun U.S. camp|newspaper=Chicago Tribune|date=10 April 1970|url=http://archives.chicagotribune.com/1970/04/10/#page/44/article/viet-reds-overrun-u-s-camp}} ;11 April A Gallup poll showed that 48% of Americans approved of Nixon's Vietnam policy while 41% disapproved.{{rp|333}} ;12 April - May Two PAVN battalions attacked [[Dak Pek Camp]] and the defenders were forced back to a small fighting position before air support forced the PAVN back. The PAVN then besieged the camp until early May when they withdrew. Total losses were 34 CIDG and 420 PAVN killed.{{cite web|url=http://www.vhpa.org/KIA/panel/battle/70041210.HTM|title=Attack on Dak Pek information for A-242 SF DET|publisher=Vietnam Helicopter Pilots' Association|access-date=14 July 2020}} ;13 April In the village of Xom Bien, a massacre of about 600 [[Vietnamese Cambodians]] was carried out by the ANK as part of a campaign by the Lon Nol government against the nation's Vietnamese-speaking minority. Shortly after midnight, troops entered the village, founded as a Roman Catholic mission on the waters of the [[Mekong River]] in the [[Chrouy Changvar Section|Chrouy Changvar]] area near Phnom Penh and removed the men and boys and shot them. Days later, hundreds of the corpses of the victims (which included more from outside of Xom Bien) were seen floating down the Mekong into South Vietnam.{{cite news|title=1,000 Civilians Slain In Cambodia— Youth Describes Massacre Of 600 Seized At Village|newspaper=Indianapolis Star|date=19 April 1970|page=1}} A PAVN sapper company attacked [[Firebase Nancy]] defended by a unit of the ARVN 1st Regiment, 1st Division and a U.S. artillery unit, returned fire and the PAVN withdrew. At dusk ARVN soldiers sweeping the perimeter made sporadic contact with PAVN.
